private_holdout_compatibility.status_correction_note: Phase 21B.4.17.2 correction (was PERMITTED_IN_PRINCIPLE): the prior reasoning ('nothing requires publication') answered the wrong question. Output ownership, stateless-API behavior, absence of a forced-publication clause, and MIT weight licensing all govern DIFFERENT rights (redistribution, IP ownership) than whether DeepSeek itself uses submitted API Input as training data for its own models -- which is the actual confidentiality-relevant question for SEALED private holdout material.
private_holdout_compatibility.authoritative_evidence_found: DeepSeek's current Privacy Policy (https://cdn.deepseek.com/policies/en-US/deepseek-privacy-policy.html, fetched 2026-09-23) states, under 'How We Use Personal Data': 'To improve and develop the Services and to train and improve our technology, such as our machine learning models and algorithms. Including by monitoring interactions and usage across your devices, analyzing how people are using it, and training and improving our technology.' This applies to 'Personal Data You Provide' including 'User Input.' The policy's carve-out ('processing rules for Personal Data collected from END USERS when accessing downstream systems or applications developed by developers using our open platform services are not covered by this privacy policy') exempts a developer's OWN end users, not the developer's own direct API traffic to DeepSeek -- confirmed by the same policy's Payment Personal Data section explicitly referencing 'when you use paid services in our open platform,' i.e. the Open Platform/API relationship IS governed by this policy. The only mitigation found is an affirmative USER right: 'the right to opt-out of using your Personal Data for training our models or optimizing our technologies' -- this is an opt-out RIGHT a user must exercise, not a default no-training posture, and no first-party documentation was found confirming (a) how/whether this opt-out applies specifically to Open Platform/API traffic as opposed to consumer chat-app usage, (b) any enterprise or zero-data-retention API tier, or (c) any Open-Platform-specific no-training/confidentiality guarantee in the Open Platform Terms of Service itself (fetched and searched this phase -- no such clause found).
private_holdout_compatibility.conclusion: No current authoritative first-party evidence establishes that API prompts sent through the DeepSeek Open Platform are treated as confidential sealed material exempt from DeepSeek's own model-training/improvement use. The Privacy Policy's affirmative training-use statement, combined with only an unexercised opt-out right and no confirmed Open-Platform-specific carve-out, means private holdout compatibility for this access path is REVIEW_REQUIRED, not PERMITTED. This is a genuine non-financial blocker distinct from (and not resolved by) the automated_evaluation_allowed=CLEAR finding in I -- that finding concerns whether ORNEUR may USE this reference for evaluation at all, not whether DeepSeek may retain/train on what ORNEUR sends it.

I_automated_evaluation_allowed.status_correction_note: Phase 21B.4.17.1 correction: the prior REVIEW_REQUIRED status searched only for the literal word 'benchmark' and treated the broader §4.2 grant as insufficient. Re-evaluated against the actual clause: ToS §4.2 affirmatively states users may apply Inputs and Outputs to 'a wide range of use cases, including personal use, academic research, derivative product development, training other models (such as model distillation), etc.' This is a broad, non-exhaustive ('etc.') grant that already names far more expansive and sensitive uses -- 'derivative product development' and 'training other models (distillation)' -- than plain automated internal evaluation/scoring. ORNEUR's Genesis frontier evaluation (sending prompts, receiving outputs, scoring them for internal comparison) is a strict subset of 'academic research' and 'derivative product development' as those terms are ordinarily understood, and is manifestly a lesser, more limited use than the distillation/training use the clause already explicitly permits. It would be internally inconsistent to read this clause as permitting the more expansive use (training a new model on outputs) while leaving the narrower, non-training use (merely evaluating and scoring outputs) unresolved.
I_automated_evaluation_allowed.rationale: The broad §4.2 affirmative grant encompasses ORNEUR's automated internal evaluation use -- CLEAR, not merely 'not prohibited.'

J_commercial_product_evaluation_allowed.rationale: MIT license places no restriction on commercial use, and ToS §4.2's broad use-case grant covers derivative product development.
